questions.stem: What is artificial pollination?
options: Inserting new genes into pollen grains to change the traits of the offspring
Moving pollen to flowers by human action, not by wind or wild animals
Producing seeds without any pollen by treating the flowers with plant hormones
Growing new plants from cuttings taken from the stems of a parent plant
questions.explanation: In artificial pollination people move pollen, by hand, with tools or with managed pollinators, so they control when and with what pollen flowers are pollinated. Cuttings are asexual propagation, with no pollen involved.

questions.stem: A plant breeder wants to cross two wheat varieties. Which method makes sure the seeds come only from the chosen parents?
options: Spray the flowers with fertiliser before any pollen is released by either variety
Remove the stigma of the female parent so that it cannot pollinate itself
Remove the female parent's anthers, bag the flowers, add chosen pollen, rebag
Plant both varieties side by side and let bees and wind pollinate them during flowering
questions.explanation: Removing the anthers prevents self-pollination, and bagging keeps out unwanted pollen, so only the pollen the breeder applies can fertilise the flowers. Without a stigma, no pollen could be received at all.

questions.stem: Australian almond growers bring in hives of honey bees each year when their orchards flower. Why?
options: Honey bees protect the almond trees from insect pests while the trees are flowering
Honey produced in the hives fertilises the soil around the roots of the almond trees
Honey bees remove extra flowers, so the nuts that remain on the trees grow larger
Almonds need insect pollination, and wild pollinators are too few
questions.explanation: Most almond varieties need pollen carried from other trees, and large orchards flower all at once, so managed hives are brought in to ensure pollination and a good nut set. The bees provide a pollination service, not pest control.

questions.stem: Why is the spread of varroa mite a concern for Australian agriculture as well as for honey producers?
options: Varroa infects crop plants directly and destroys their flowers before pollination occurs
Varroa makes honey bees so aggressive that farmers cannot work in their fields
Varroa competes with crop plants for nutrients in the soil around the orchards
Many crops rely on honey bee pollination, and varroa kills colonies
questions.explanation: Varroa mites feed on bees and spread viruses, and unmanaged feral colonies, which pollinate many crops for free, usually die out. Growers then depend more on managed hives, raising pollination costs.

questions.stem: Which is an outcome of artificial pollination in plant breeding?
options: Clones that are genetically identical to one of the two parent plants
Plants that no longer need water or nutrients from the soil to grow
Seeds that contain no DNA at all from the plant that supplied the pollen
New varieties combining traits such as disease resistance and yield
questions.explanation: Controlled crosses combine alleles from two chosen parents, so breeders can select offspring with useful combinations of traits. The offspring are not clones; they carry DNA from both parents.

questions.stem: Growing a few high-yielding varieties bred by artificial pollination over very large areas can reduce crop genetic diversity. Why is this a risk?
options: A new pest or disease could damage most of the crop at once
Crops with low diversity cannot be harvested by machinery
Low genetic diversity makes plants produce poisonous seeds
Uniform crops need much more water than diverse crops
questions.explanation: If most plants share the same alleles, a pathogen able to overcome one plant can attack nearly all of them, as happened when Panama disease devastated uniform banana crops. Diversity spreads the risk.

questions.stem: Bumblebees are not permitted on mainland Australia, so many glasshouse tomato growers vibrate the flowers with hand-held electric devices. Why does this work?
options: Tomato flowers release their pollen when shaken, as bumblebees do by buzzing
The vibration kills the fungi that would otherwise infect the tomato flowers
The device injects pollen from another plant species into each tomato flower
The vibration makes the tomato fruit develop without any fertilisation
questions.explanation: Tomato anthers hold pollen in tubes that release it when vibrated, which bumblebees do naturally by buzz pollination; the device imitates this so pollen reaches the stigma. Fruit then develops after fertilisation.

questions.stem: An orchard study finds fruit set of 10% in flowers bagged to exclude insects, 35% in open flowers and 55% in hand-pollinated flowers. What do these data suggest?
options: Hand pollination damages flowers, which is why fruit set is reduced in the open
Fruit set depends on the bags used, because bagged flowers have a warmer climate
Pollination limits fruit set, and natural pollination is falling short
Insects reduce fruit set, because they damage flowers while they collect pollen
questions.explanation: Excluding insects lowers fruit set, so insects are pollinating, but adding pollen by hand raises it further, showing that open flowers receive less pollen than they could use. Growers might add hives or hand pollinate.

questions.stem: Why are seeds dried and stored at very low temperatures in a seed bank?
options: To make the seeds germinate faster once they are sown
To soften the seed coat so that it can be removed
To slow their metabolism so that they stay viable for decades
To kill any embryos that carry harmful recessive alleles
questions.explanation: Drying and freezing slow the chemical reactions that age a seed, so many seeds survive for decades and can be grown when needed for research or restoration.

questions.stem: Some rainforest plants have seeds that die if they are dried, so they cannot be stored in a normal seed bank. How can these species still be conserved?
options: By storing the seeds dried out at room temperature for many years
By grinding the seeds into a powder and storing it in sealed jars
By waiting for the plants to evolve seeds that tolerate drying
By storing embryos or shoot tips in liquid nitrogen
questions.explanation: Cryopreservation stores small pieces of living tissue at about minus 196 degrees Celsius, stopping metabolism; the tissue can later be regrown by tissue culture. Drying kills these seeds, which is why the standard method fails.

questions.stem: The Wollemi pine was discovered in 1994, with fewer than 100 adult trees in the wild. Cuttings and tissue culture were used to grow many plants for sale and for planting elsewhere. How has this helped conserve it?
options: It reduced pressure on the wild trees and spread the species across many sites
It greatly increased the genetic diversity of the trees in the wild population
It allowed scientists to bring back the extinct ancestor of the Wollemi pine
It removed the need to protect the location of the wild trees from people
questions.explanation: Making the plants widely available reduced the incentive to visit or take material from the wild site, and plantings elsewhere act as insurance against fire or disease. Propagation copies existing plants, so it does not add diversity.

questions.stem: Why is propagating a rare plant only by cuttings or tissue culture a limited conservation strategy?
options: Clones always die before they are old enough to reproduce
Cuttings carry far more mutations than seeds from the same plant
Plants grown by tissue culture are unable to photosynthesise
The new plants are clones, so genetic diversity is not increased
questions.explanation: Asexual propagation copies the parent's genotype, so a population of clones remains vulnerable to any pest or disease that affects that genotype. Sexual reproduction or collecting from many individuals is needed to maintain diversity.

questions.stem: Seed collected from many plants of a threatened species is grown and planted at several new sites. What is the main conservation benefit?
options: A single fire or disease is less likely to wipe out the whole species
Every new plant is a clone of the healthiest plant in the population
Planting at new sites prevents the species from ever being pollinated
The species no longer needs any protection at its original site
questions.explanation: Establishing populations in several places spreads the risk of loss, and using seed from many plants keeps a wide range of alleles in the new populations. The original site still needs protection.

questions.stem: What is environmental DNA (eDNA)?
options: DNA found only in the nucleus of plant cells, not of animal cells
DNA from extinct species stored in the collections of museums
DNA shed into water, soil or air that can be sampled
DNA made in the laboratory to genetically modify crop plants
questions.explanation: Organisms constantly shed cells, mucus, faeces and other material containing DNA into their surroundings, so a sample of water or soil holds traces of the species living there.

questions.stem: Water samples from a river are filtered, and the DNA collected is sequenced and compared with reference databases. What can this show about the river's ecosystem?
options: The temperature and pH of the water at each of the sampling points
Which species are present, including hidden ones, without catching them
The exact number of individuals of each species that lives in the river
The age of each fish and frog that has lived in the river this year
questions.explanation: Matching sequences to databases identifies the species whose DNA is in the sample, so surveys can detect rare or elusive species and track changes over time. eDNA gives presence, not accurate counts or ages.

questions.stem: An eDNA survey fails to detect a frog species known to live in a creek. Which is the most likely explanation?
options: Frog cells contain no DNA, so they cannot leave any trace in the water
Frog DNA dissolves in water instantly and so is never left in creeks
Its sequence is not in the database, or too little DNA was sampled
eDNA methods can detect fish species but never amphibians such as frogs
questions.explanation: A species is identified only if its sequence is in the reference database and enough of its DNA is captured; low numbers, timing or DNA breakdown can cause false negatives. eDNA works for any organism that sheds DNA.

questions.stem: How can sequencing the microbes in soil samples help determine the health of an ecosystem?
options: Shifts in microbe types and diversity can signal pollution
It shows how many trees grew in the soil in each year of the past century
It records the rainfall that fell on the area over the past decade
It reveals which animals were hunted by predators in the area
questions.explanation: Soil microbes drive nutrient cycling and respond quickly to disturbance, so a shift in their communities, identified by comparing sequences with databases, is an early sign of change in ecosystem health.

questions.stem: The koala genome was sequenced in 2018. How can genomic data like this inform conservation decisions?
options: By measuring population genetic diversity to guide translocation
By allowing koalas to be cloned from museum specimens to replace wild populations
By replacing the need to protect koala habitat, as numbers can be predicted from DNA
By showing the exact age and life expectancy of every koala in the wild
questions.explanation: Genome data let researchers compare populations, identify those with low diversity or distinct genetic makeup, and study genes linked to diseases such as chlamydia, guiding which animals to move or breed. Habitat protection remains essential.

questions.stem: DNA from scats shows that a small, isolated population of a threatened marsupial has low heterozygosity. Which management action do these data most support?
options: Removing the oldest animals so that the youngest face less competition
Leaving the population alone, as low heterozygosity shows it is healthy
Bringing in animals from a genetically different population
Moving the whole population into captivity and stopping all breeding
questions.explanation: Low heterozygosity signals inbreeding and lost diversity, which gene flow from another population can reverse, as genetic rescue. Stopping breeding or culling would not restore lost alleles.

questions.stem: Why do researchers often collect DNA from scats or hair rather than capturing rare animals?
options: Hair contains no DNA, so it cannot contaminate other samples
Capturing wild animals is illegal everywhere in Australia
It avoids stressing rare animals while still giving genetic data
Scat DNA is far more complete than DNA taken from blood samples
questions.explanation: Non-invasive samples contain enough DNA to identify individuals, sex and genetic diversity, without the risks of trapping and handling. Their DNA is usually lower in quality than blood, not better.

questions.stem: How does marker-assisted selection use bioinformatics in crop breeding?
options: DNA markers linked to desired traits are used to pick young seedlings
Seedlings are injected with markers that make them grow into the desired variety
Markers are painted onto mature plants to show which ones farmers prefer
Computer models replace the need to grow any of the plants in the field
questions.explanation: Sequence data identify DNA markers that are inherited along with useful genes, so breeders can test young seedlings and keep only those carrying the marker, saving years of growing. No genes are inserted.

questions.stem: What is Golden Rice engineered to produce in its grain?
options: Extra iron, which prevents anaemia in children
Human insulin, for people with type 1 diabetes
Beta-carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A
Vitamin C, which prevents the disease scurvy
questions.explanation: Golden Rice makes beta-carotene, the orange-yellow pigment the body converts to vitamin A, which gives the grain its golden colour. It was designed to address vitamin A deficiency.

questions.stem: Why was Golden Rice developed?
options: To reduce vitamin A deficiency, which can cause blindness
To allow rice to grow well in salty soils near the coast in tropical regions
To make rice plants resistant to insect pests without the need for spraying
To reduce the very large amount of water that rice crops normally need
questions.explanation: In communities where rice is the main food, vitamin A deficiency is common and causes night blindness, blindness and greater risk of death from infections, especially in children. Golden Rice targets this through the staple food.

questions.stem: Rice plants make beta-carotene in their leaves but not in their grain. What did scientists do to make Golden Rice?
options: Selectively bred the rice plants with the most yellow leaves over many generations
Sprayed the rice grain with a solution of beta-carotene shortly before harvest
Removed the genes for making starch, so beta-carotene builds up in the grain
Inserted genes for enzymes that complete the beta-carotene pathway in the grain
questions.explanation: Genes for two enzymes, one from maize or daffodil and one from a bacterium, were inserted with a promoter active in the endosperm, so the grain completes the pathway to beta-carotene. Selective breeding could not achieve this, because rice has no alleles for it in the grain.

questions.stem: Golden Rice contains a gene from maize and a gene from a bacterium. How is it classified?
options: A hybrid produced by artificial pollination
A transgenic organism, and therefore also a GMO
A GMO, but not a transgenic organism
Neither, because the genes came from food species
questions.explanation: Its genome was altered by gene technology, making it a GMO, and it carries genes from other species, making it transgenic. A hybrid comes from crossing, not gene insertion.

questions.stem: Which is an ethical concern raised about Golden Rice?
options: It can be grown only in laboratories, never in farmers' fields
It may treat a symptom of poverty rather than improving diet diversity
It contains enough vitamin A to cause poisoning in anyone who eats it
Eating it transfers the inserted genes into the cells of the consumer
questions.explanation: Critics argue that money might be better spent improving access to varied diets and supplements, and raise questions about corporate control of crops, although Golden Rice has been made available free to poor farmers. The body converts beta-carotene only as needed, and eaten DNA is digested.

questions.stem: Which is a benefit of using a GM staple crop to address a nutritional deficiency?
options: It works even if the crop is never grown or eaten by anyone
It permanently changes the DNA of the people who eat it
It reaches people through foods they already eat
It removes the need for any other foods in a person's diet
questions.explanation: A biofortified staple delivers the nutrient as part of the normal diet, which suits communities with limited access to supplements or varied foods. It supplements a diet; it does not alter the consumer's genes.

questions.stem: Herbicide-tolerant GM canola is grown near weedy relatives that can cross with it. What is a possible impact on natural populations?
options: The tolerance gene could spread to weedy relatives, making them hard to kill
The weedy relatives would become completely unable to reproduce with each other
The canola plants would turn into a native species within a few generations
The herbicide would stop working on every plant species in the surrounding area
questions.explanation: Pollen can carry the tolerance gene into related plants that interbreed with canola, producing herbicide-tolerant weeds. This gene flow is one of the risks assessed before a GMO is released.

questions.stem: Growers of Bt cotton in Australia must also plant refuge crops that lack the Bt gene. Why?
options: So the cotton yield is lowered deliberately and the price of cotton rises
So susceptible insects survive to mate with resistant ones
So the Bt gene can spread from the cotton into the plants grown in the refuge
So beneficial insects in the refuge are killed by the Bt toxin as well
questions.explanation: Bt toxin selects for resistant pests; refuges keep a large population of susceptible insects, whose matings with any resistant survivors keep resistance alleles rare. This applies natural selection to manage a GMO's long-term use.

questions.stem: A gene drive is designed to spread a gene causing female infertility through an invasive pest population. What is a key risk of releasing it?
options: It could spread to populations where the species is native or valued
It would make the pest population grow faster because fewer females compete
It would affect only the individuals released and never spread to offspring
It would change the pest into a different species within a single generation
questions.explanation: Gene drives are built to spread through a species far faster than normal inheritance, so if individuals move, the gene could reach populations elsewhere, with effects that are hard to reverse. Such drives are designed to spread to offspring.

questions.stem: In Australia, which body assesses the risks to people and the environment of releasing a GMO?
options: The Office of the Gene Technology Regulator
Food Standards Australia New Zealand
The Therapeutic Goods Administration
The Australian Bureau of Statistics
questions.explanation: The Gene Technology Regulator licenses dealings with GMOs, including field trials and commercial release, after assessing risks to health and the environment. Food Standards Australia New Zealand assesses the safety of GM food, and the Therapeutic Goods Administration regulates medicines.

questions.stem: Tasmania has kept a moratorium on growing GM crops. Which economic reason is commonly given for it?
options: Tasmanian law bans every form of plant breeding, including crossing
To market its produce as GM-free to buyers willing to pay more for it
GM crops are unable to grow in Tasmania's cool and wet climate
GM seed is given away free, which would cut seed company profits
questions.explanation: Being GM-free is seen as a marketing advantage for Tasmanian food in some export and domestic markets. This is an economic and social decision, not a sign that GM crops cannot grow there.

questions.stem: Why might a small farmer in a developing country be unable to adopt a GM crop even if it gives higher yields?
options: GM crops can be grown only on farms larger than a thousand hectares
GM seed cannot be transported to countries outside Australia
Patented seed may be costly and may need to be bought every season
GM crops need no water or fertiliser, so the farmer has nothing to buy
questions.explanation: Seed companies recover research costs through patents and licence fees, and growers often may not save seed, so the cost can be a barrier. Some humanitarian GM crops are licensed free to small farmers to address this.

questions.stem: A community rejects a GM variety of its traditional staple crop, although regulators found it safe and more nutritious. Which kind of influence does this most likely reflect?
options: Scientific, such as new evidence showing the crop is unsafe
Climatic, such as the crop failing in the local weather
Cultural, such as beliefs about traditional foods and farming
Economic, such as lower prices for the more nutritious crop
questions.explanation: Food is tied to identity, tradition and values about nature, so communities may reject a modified staple even when it is safe. The stem states the crop was found safe, so a scientific objection is not the cause.

questions.stem: Why does Food Standards Australia New Zealand require most GM foods to be labelled?
options: Because the labels break down the modified DNA in the food
So that consumers can make informed choices about what they eat
Because GM foods have been found unsafe for people to eat
So that GM foods can always be sold at higher prices than others
questions.explanation: GM foods are assessed for safety before sale, and labelling gives consumers information to choose according to their own values. Labelling is a social response to public concern, not a safety warning.

questions.stem: Which combination of factors would most favour the adoption of a new drought-tolerant GM wheat by Australian growers?
options: No regulatory approval, but strong support from a few large buyers
Low yields in dry years, and labelling rules that deter consumers
Regulatory approval, export markets that accept it, and affordable seed
Consumer rejection, very high seed costs and bans in export markets
questions.explanation: Adoption depends on legal approval, on buyers at home and overseas accepting the product, and on seed prices that make it worthwhile, so regulation, markets and economics all shape whether a biotechnology is used.
